solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Second option mostly involving ultimate academic

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for second

indicators.note: to involve something is to take it in, so one piece wraps round another

parts.note: an option is a choice, cut short by one letter
ultimate means last

explanation.surface: A university picks its second choice, which happens to involve a leading scholar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ultimate academic' wants to be a top scholar, but 'ultimate' is wordplay and 'academic' alone is the definition, an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Both adjectives describe things relating to schools, learning and formal study, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Court accommodating former King and old Emperor?

indicators.note: accommodating means giving room to, so one piece is housed inside another

parts.note: CT is the abbreviation for court
former, as in at one time, is once
R for Rex, Latin for king
O is a standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A royal court that once housed a deposed king and an ancient emperor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Former King' reads as an ex-monarch but is two separate pieces. The question mark flags that 'Emperor' is a nickname, not a ruler.
explanation.definitionFit: The 'Emperor' is the popular title of Beethoven's fifth piano concerto, so it is one example of the musical form.

clue.text: Lines up one to head paper round

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read from bottom to top, the opposite way

parts.note: the person heading a newspaper is the editor, ED
a round shape is the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone queues up to lead the paper round, like a keen delivery child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paper round' looks like a newspaper delivery route, but 'round' is O and 'one to head paper' is the editor.
explanation.definitionFit: A poem is made of lines of verse, and an ode is a lyric poem, so it is an example of lines.

clue.text: Upset PA sees head of team leaving

indicators.note: something leaving goes away, so that letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: Tannoy is a British brand name used for any public address system

indicators.note: the head of something is its top, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of this word

explanation.surface: A personal assistant is upset to see the team leader walk out.
explanation.walkthrough: PA looks like a personal assistant, but it is a public address system; in Britain a Tannoy is the loudspeaker system at stations and stadiums. Remove its T to get ANNOY.
explanation.definitionFit: To upset someone is to irritate or bother them, so the verbs are close synonyms.

clue.text: Significant narration

definitions.meaning: first meaning: revealing or having a marked effect
second meaning: the act of recounting a story

explanation.walkthrough: Two words, two unrelated meanings of one word: an adjective for meaningful and a noun for recounting.
explanation.definitionFit: A revealing detail is called this, and recounting a story is the noun form of the verb meaning to relate.

clue.text: Close friend cooked and brought in meat dish

indicators.note: to be brought in is to be placed within, so one piece goes inside another
cooking transforms ingredients, so these letters are reworked

parts.note: the letters of this little word rearranged
confit is meat such as duck slow-cooked in its own fat

explanation.surface: A friend made a meal and brought in a meat dish to share.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooked' sits naturally beside 'meat dish' but it works on 'and'; the result goes inside CONFIT.
explanation.definitionFit: A confidant is a trusted person one shares secrets with, so an intimate companion.

clue.text: Damp, but not the second source of damp

indicators.note: not the second tells us to remove the letter in second position

parts.note: damp means moist

explanation.surface: A puzzling line about something damp that is not the second cause of dampness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Damp' appears twice: the first is wordplay giving MOIST, whose second letter O goes, leaving MIST.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine water droplets hanging in the air leave everything they touch wet, so this is a cause of moisture.

clue.text: Imports business reduced by half reorganised in one-sided arrangement

indicators.note: cut by half means only the first half of the letters remain
reorganising puts things into a new order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
the first four of this word's eight letters

explanation.surface: An importing firm, cut in half and restructured, ends up in a lopsided deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One-sided arrangement' reads like an unfair deal, but it describes a mathematical surface with only one side.
explanation.definitionFit: A Möbius strip is a band given a half-twist before its ends are joined, giving a surface with a single face.

clue.text: Welcome line in fried food

indicators.note: in places one thing inside the other

parts.note: sauté describes food quickly fried in a pan
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A welcome line of fried snacks, as at a party buffet.
explanation.walkthrough: The L goes inside SAUTE to give SALUTE.
explanation.definitionFit: To greet someone formally with a gesture is to receive them, so the verbs share a sense of greeting.

clue.text: Deduce computer network turned evil

parts.note: to deduce is to infer

indicators.note: something turned faces the other way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a LAN is a local area network

explanation.surface: Someone concludes that the computer network has become malevolent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned evil' reads as one phrase, but 'turned' acts only on the network.
explanation.definitionFit: Infernal literally means belonging to hell, so it is used for anything devilish or wicked.

clue.text: Crab, perhaps, unable to be cracked

indicators.note: something cracked breaks open, so the letters fall into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A crab whose shell cannot be broken open.
explanation.walkthrough: Cracking a crab's shell is the natural picture, which hides the signal; the crab is not a crustacean at all.
explanation.definitionFit: The Crab is a famous cloud of gas and dust in Taurus, so it is an example of this astronomical object.

clue.text: Main route all but fixed from here

indicators.note: all but means everything except the final letter

parts.note: fixed is set, short of its last letter
away means at a distance from this place

explanation.surface: Directions saying the main road is almost entirely repaired from this point on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' looks like principal, but it is the old word for the open sea, as in the Spanish Main.
explanation.definitionFit: The main is a poetic term for the ocean, so a route across it is a shipping lane for vessels.

clue.text: A little attention around college regarding office work

parts.note: a whit is a tiny amount

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: to give someone your ear is to pay attention
Coll. is the abbreviation for college

explanation.surface: A college asks for some attention to be paid to its admin staff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lend me your ear' is the idea behind attention here; 'regarding' belongs to the definition, which describes rather than names.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes clerical and professional jobs done at desks, as opposed to manual labour.

clue.text: Island I leave to probe US city villainy

parts.note: I is the abbreviation for island

indicators.note: probing means going inside, so one piece is inserted into another

parts.note: NY is New York
to leave is to quit, so I leave is I quit

explanation.surface: Someone quits an island to investigate crime in an American city.
explanation.walkthrough: I, then I QUIT inside NY.
explanation.definitionFit: Both nouns mean wickedness or grossly immoral behaviour, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Spoiled girl embracing grand feature of church

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold in your arms, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: spoiled by marks is stained
a lass is a girl
G is short for grand, a thousand

explanation.surface: A spoilt girl hugs her grandmother at the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoiled girl' looks like one person, but 'Spoiled' is a separate piece; LASS takes in G.
explanation.definitionFit: Coloured glass windows depicting saints and scenes are a characteristic part of church architecture.

clue.text: Not initially unbranded, about to become active

indicators.note: not initially means without the opening letter
about means surrounding, so one piece goes round another

parts.note: unbranded goods are generic, here without their first letter
to get, as in get angry, is to become

explanation.surface: A product that was not unbranded at first is about to be launched.
explanation.walkthrough: GENERIC loses its G and the remainder goes around GET.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone full of vigour and vitality is lively and busy, so the adjectives are synonyms.

clue.text: Isn't upset over a new church, for example

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters land out of order

parts.note: the word without its apostrophe
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A complaint that someone is not upset about a new church being built.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For example' looks like the definition, but only 'example' is; 'for' links it to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An instance is a single case cited to illustrate a point, as in the phrase for instance.

clue.text: Token of love in entirety, playing Wagner operas

indicators.note: playing suggests performing freely, so the letters are moved around

parts.note: taken as written
Wagner's Ring cycle is a set of four operas

explanation.surface: A devoted fan expresses love by playing all of Wagner's operas in full.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing Wagner operas' reads as a performance, but 'playing' looks back at 'entirety'.
explanation.definitionFit: This ring set with a continuous band of stones is given as a gift symbolising lasting devotion.

clue.text: No poles: circus tent continuing to move?

parts.note: taken as written
the north and south poles
the big top is a circus tent

explanation.surface: A circus tent with no poles keeps shifting about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No poles' suggests a collapsing tent, but the poles are the compass points N and S.
explanation.definitionFit: Something going on without any break or halt in its motion is uninterrupted.

clue.text: Descriptive of stones or tablets?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: made of small pieces of stone set in a pattern
second meaning: relating to Moses, who brought down the tablets of the Law

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stones or tablets' looks like pills of different kinds; the second sense is the capitalised adjective for Moses, whose commandments were carved on stone tablets.
explanation.definitionFit: Small tesserae of stone form patterned artwork, and the Ten Commandments given to Moses were written on tablets.

clue.text: Extremely good, more than once, about British article in winter sports equipment

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: too means excessively
B is the abbreviation for British
G for good, given twice
an indefinite article

explanation.surface: A gushing review of a British-made item of ski gear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely good' looks like a phrase meaning the first and last letters of good; it is TOO plus G, and 'more than once' doubles the G. TOO goes around B.
explanation.definitionFit: A long narrow sled for sliding downhill on snow is a piece of winter sporting kit.

clue.text: In the past, you'd backed including place for second-in-command

indicators.note: including means taking in, so one piece sits inside another
something backed goes in reverse, so its letters run the other way

parts.note: the archaic form of you'd is ye'd
to place is to put

explanation.surface: Someone recalls once backing a candidate for the vice-chair position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the past' reads as time-setting, but it turns you'd into its old-fashioned form, with ye for you.
explanation.definitionFit: A deputy acts for and ranks directly beneath a chief, so the nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Energetic figure from cycling world in France

indicators.note: cycling means going round in a loop, so letters move from one end to the other

parts.note: monde is French for world

explanation.surface: A dynamic star of the cycling world in France, as at the Tour de France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' fits the Tour de France picture, but it moves the last two letters of MONDE to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A demon at something, as in a demon bowler, is a person of ferocious vigour or skill.

clue.text: Play for which actor given licence

parts.note: a ham is an overacting performer
let means allowed, given permission

explanation.surface: A play that needed a performing licence before an actor could appear in it.
explanation.walkthrough: HAM then LET.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's tragedy about the Prince of Denmark is among the best-known dramas in English.

clue.text: Money received by office worker: good, attractive

parts.note: a temp is a temporary office worker
tin is British slang for money
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: Good pay for an office worker makes a job appealing.
explanation.walkthrough: Money received by the worker puts the cash after the worker; tin is old British slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tempting entices you and appeals strongly to desire, so it is alluring.

clue.text: Drop of salt water, not right for drink

indicators.note: not right means without the letter standing for right

parts.note: a teardrop is salty water

explanation.surface: A drop of seawater is unsuitable for drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Salt water' suggests the sea, but the drop is from the eye; TEAR loses R.
explanation.definitionFit: The infusion of dried leaves in hot water is a common beverage.

clue.text: Horrific cut — may result in this

definitions.text: Horrific cut — may result in this

indicators.note: to cut is to trim, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: horrific means scary, here docked

explanation.surface: A warning that a nasty wound may leave a lasting mark.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as wordplay, 'cut' trims SCARY; read whole, the clue describes the answer as what a bad wound leaves behind.
explanation.definitionFit: A wound heals with fibrous tissue that leaves a permanent visible mark on the skin.

clue.text: European capital willing to consider form of change externally

indicators.note: a form of something is a version of it, so these letters take a new shape
externally means on the outside, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: the six letters rearranged
open to an idea is willing to consider it

explanation.surface: A European capital weighing up some form of change to its outer districts.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged CHANGE wraps around OPEN, splitting after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Copenhagen is the capital city of Denmark, so it is one example of a capital in Europe.
